I inherited cast iron cookware from two grandmothers and my Mom and was well indoctrinated to the seasoning process. However they are pretty hard to really screw up and I use the sanding and resurfacing technique mentioned above but without the fried rice thing. That makes sense though.

My GF also has a pretty good cast iron collection from her family but she never got the 'no soap' indoctrination. I have gotten pissed to catch her letting one of 'my' perfectly seasoned skillets sit in the sink with a big squirt of Dawn overnight. We once got into a big fight when she claimed that the soaking skillet was her Mothers and not one of mine. I can tell one of mine just by looking at the patina of the metal and I threatened to get all of mine engraved with my initials. It all got pretty stupid and I finally grabbed the violated skillet out of the sink and stepped to the kitchen door and flung it as far as I could into the white salt enriched beach sand telling her that the salty sand was better for the cooking surface than the soap. I left it out in the rain and salt air of our bayou for a couple of weeks before going through the seasoning process.

I also have an Australian 'Jaffle Maker' in cast iron which I have never used enough to get a really good seasoning on. Often known as a 'pie iron' they were a favorite among the surfer culture as you and you buddies could by a loaf of Wonder Bread and a can of Pork and Beans and make bean and bacon turnovers over a beach fire. Cheap meal for sure.

One thing I'm really fond of is the ability to get the cast iron ripping hot for a sear and then in the same pan it goes into the oven or onto the grill to cook whatever.

Memories of my Mom baking pineapple upside down cake in the cast iron skillet. Nothing like it…those southern women know how to cook.

Food Wishes' John Armand Mitzewich, more commonly known as "Chef John", is an American chef who puts together very tasty easy to make recipes. Since retiring we eat beef a couple times a month at the most. When we eat beef, we prefer something from the rib - rib steak, boneless rib steak or prime rib. Once in a great while we'll use another cut of beef for making a stew or one of the Chili recipes I use, or choose beef brisket or corned beef for our Saint Patrick's dinner of corned beef and cabbage, or making Reuben sandwiches.

We have way to much beef in the freezer, since my son, who processes through beef he's raised, and brings over boxs of beef directly from his butcher. My wife put's anything rib aside, pulls out a few specialty cuts, and gives the rest to the neighbors. She pulled out a Tri-tip, and asked which way we should cook it. Chef John has a very easy Tri-tip recipe, that'll treat most beef lovers palate.

Tri-tip is very versatile and flavorful, goes well in the grill, in the oven, or even in a pressure pot.

Once I chose Chef John's recipe, Linda went to the garden and cut some fresh rosemary, while I made the rub, did the prep, placed it in a oval cast iron roasting pan, one can use a rectangular cast iron or metal roasting pan - cook's choice. Let it set for a while after rubbing in the rub, then put it in the oven, on 225° F for an hour and a half, and let rest covered for 20 minutes. This recipe is mouth-watering tasty.

Chef John should be a national celebrity (if he wants to be). His recipes are always the best, many of which can be cooked in cast iron or not....

Ingredients For the Rub:

2 tablespoons kosher salt

1 tablespoon freshly ground black pepper

1 tablespoon smoked paprika

1 teaspoon garlic powder

¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper

1 teaspoon dried rosemary

1 tablespoon chopped fresh rosemary leaves

1 (2 1/2 pound) beef tri-tip roast

Directions

Step 1

Preheat the oven to 225 degrees F (110 degrees C).

Step 2

Mix salt, pepper, paprika, garlic powder, cayenne, dried rosemary, and fresh rosemary together in a small bowl.

Step 3

Place tri-tip in a baking pan. Season generously with the spice rub until both sides are completely covered.

Step 4

Bake in the preheated oven until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 130 degrees F (54 degrees C) for medium-rare, or until desired doneness, 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Flip meat over halfway.

Step 5

Cover pan with aluminum foil and let meat rest for 20 minutes. Remove tri-tip to a cutting board and cut into 2 pieces along where the grain changes direction. Slice meat across the grain and transfer to serving plates.

Step 6

Mix beef broth in with the pan drippings and drizzle over the slices

Those whom know me, know I like a Reuben, made with Corned Beef or Smoked Beef Brisket. The very best Reuben is made with Corned Beef and Pastrami. Both meats come from the same cut of beef (brisket) and are brined for up to a week, but afterwards corned beef is boiled while pastrami is seasoned with a dry spice mix and smoked. In a pinch with no Corned Beef on hand, Pastrami can be used as the only meat. If you want to get technical, a Reuben sandwich made with pastrami is called a “Rachel”. A classic Reuben is always made with corned beef!

However, I prefer to make a Reuben with both Corned Beef and Pastrami, Swiss Cheese, Sauerkraut, on Dill Rye or Russian Rye in a pinch. Russian dressing is preferred with one side also having a spread of regular mustard and the other a spread of horseradish over the Russian Dressing, with each side getting a couple slices of Swiss Cheese. Then a couple tablespoons of Sauerkraut on one side and some healthy slices of Corned Beef and slices of Pastrami on the other side - or you can build the whole sandwich on one side. Then put both sides together and grill till brown and crispy, on a cast iron skillet, though you can grill on a steel skillet.

Despite Russian dressing and Thousand Island dressing being quite similar, a classic Reuben is traditionally made with Russian dressing.

Both sauces begin with a base of mayo and ketchup, which result in a pink color. But the main difference lays on the fact that Thousand Island is sweeter and studded with pickle relish, while Russian dressing is a bit spicier, with a little heat from horseradish and hot sauce.

And while you can certainly find both of those dressings at your local grocery store, making them at home is very easy!

A Russian dressing recipe consists of mixing mayonnaise, ketchup (or ketchup-style chili sauce), horseradish, hot sauce, Worcestershire sauce, sweetpaprika, a tablespoon of chopped or grated onion ( I prefer shallot) and salt.

Now, if you’re a Thousand Island guy (or gal) and already have that in your fridge, by all means, use that! You can even add a few dashes of hot sauce to make it spicier and closer to Russian dressing.

The very best Reuban made around this side of the water is at the Blue Moose Cafe in Port Townsend, across the street from the Port Townsend Shipwrights Co-op. They have their Beef Brisket smoked locally in Port Townsend and make their own special bread for the Ruben.

Now for my second favorite sandwich, a Cubano, watch this video by Chef John, because it shows the proper way to make a Cubano, though I add 2-3 times as much Cayenne when I make my sauce.
